Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette:
Arjun Patel is a 35-year-old tax consultant who came to treatment after months of telling his wife he was “just tired” and that work stress was catching up with him. Before returning to the U.S., he had spent several weeks as a relief worker in a war zone, helping distribute supplies and assisting with evacuations after shelling in a civilian area. The moment that now sits at the center of his distress is fragmented in his telling: he remembers smoke hanging low over a damaged street, people shouting, and moving toward a building where families had been sheltering. He recalls seeing bodies brought out, the air thick with burning and dust, and being forced to choose who could be moved first. A burial area had formed nearby because there was nowhere else to take the dead. What stays with him most is the conviction that others were looking to him and that he did not do enough.

Since returning home, seemingly ordinary moments in his daily life as a tax consultant have become charged with danger. If he passes a cluster of smokers outside his office building, the smell of smoke catches in his throat and his whole body reacts before he can think. If a client raises their voice in irritation, even calmly, he feels himself tense and brace. When a colleague mentioned attending a funeral for her father, he had to leave the break room. These moments do not stay small. The smell, the word funeral, the sight of anger on someone’s face immediately pull up pieces of the war-zone scene, and he can suddenly feel his body folding into the same protective crouch he had taken there, his hands drawn up toward his face as if shielding himself.

The memories come in a disjointed way that unsettles him further. He cannot place what happened in a clear sequence, only broken images and bodily sensations. At night, when the house is quiet, he finds it harder to feel safe than during the day; the dark seems to leave too much room for something to happen. Ordinary sounds—a car door slamming outside, the heating system clicking on—make him jump sharply, and afterwards the half-formed memories push closer. Living at that pitch of alarm gradually convinced him that his fear was telling the truth: that he was no longer someone who could count on safety, and that ordinary life itself had become precarious. In those moments he is not only remembering smoke and shouted instructions; he is flooded with shame, gripped by the sense that he had been in the position to protect people and failed.

That meaning has spread far beyond the event itself. Arjun has come to believe that the world no longer works according to any dependable rules, that catastrophe can arrive without warning and that decency offers no protection. Holding that belief, he moved through ordinary days as if they were full of signals he could not afford to miss; a raised voice in the office, smoke on someone’s clothes, even the mention of a funeral snagged his attention as possible signs that the same kind of catastrophe was close again. He feels cut off from other people, including friends who try to welcome him back into normal routines. When triggers hit—a funeral notice online, smoke from a neighbor’s grill, a flash of irritation in someone’s voice—they do not just evoke memory; they confirm what he now believes about himself and the world. He hears in another person’s anger the same helpless urgency of those days overseas, and he reads his own reaction as proof that he is fundamentally different from everyone around him.

Over time he has organized his life around trying not to feel any of this. Those efforts ended up drawing the boundaries of the trauma through his week: the streets he no longer took, the conversations he cut short, and the family events he declined all became reminders in their own right, keeping funerals, smoke, and anger continually marked out in his mind. He avoids the part of the city where a humanitarian fundraiser was held because it reminds him of the field site and the people he could not save. When something upsetting catches him off guard, he covers his face with his hands, a gesture that briefly blocks the room around him but also puts him back into the body posture of the event. He has also begun turning away from invitations that might make him feel good—his wife’s plans for dinners out, celebrations with cousins, even a weekend trip—because hope and pleasure feel almost disloyal. If he lets himself enjoy anything, he fears he is erasing the dead or excusing his failure. These habits have narrowed his life, and in the narrowing he feels even more separate and ashamed.

The strategies that are meant to keep him steady seem instead to tighten everything. Because he so often escaped, covered his face, checked, or stayed away before finding out he was actually safe, his body never had reason to revise its alarm; the very things he did to get through the moment left danger feeling current and unresolved. Avoiding reminders leaves the memories more confused and jagged, never fully sorted into the past. Covering his face when distressed makes the bodily sense of the event more immediate. Staying away from happy occasions has strained his marriage; his wife experiences him as absent and unreachable, which he silently takes as further evidence that he does not belong with other people anymore. At work, his concentration has worsened during client meetings, especially late in the day or after being startled by a noise in the office, and he has become increasingly vigilant by evening, checking locks and scanning sounds outside the apartment. Already braced for danger, he found that more and more of the world registered as warning; by the end of a workday, ambiguous noises in the hallway, a stranger lingering near the building entrance, or irritation in a client’s tone could all flare into reminders.

What finally brought Arjun in was a recent family funeral. He had agreed to attend for the sake of his parents, but the smell of incense and cremation smoke, the gathered grief, and a relative’s curt voice sent him spiraling into a familiar collapse of body memory, shame, and alarm. He spent much of the service with his face in his hands, then left abruptly and sat in his car shaking. He told his wife afterward that he was afraid he was becoming someone who could no longer live in ordinary life—someone always waiting for the next sign of danger, always one reminder away from that street. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is not to forget what happened, but to be able to remember it without feeling condemned by it.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly show Arjun’s negative appraisals causing him to become more sensitive to or generate triggers/reminders.
The vignette shows threat and alarm occurring alongside shame and beliefs, but it does not explicitly convey that his sense of threat leads to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not explicitly state that Arjun’s sense of threat increases attention to, sensitivity to, or creation of triggers/reminders.

Although avoidance and other maladaptive strategies are described as narrowing his life, the vignette does not clearly state that these strategies lead to increased exposure to or sensitivity to triggers/reminders.
The vignette describes maladaptive strategies maintaining memories and shame, but it does not explicitly convey that these strategies heighten Arjun’s sense of threat or danger.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show Arjun’s negative appraisals causing him to become more sensitive to or generate triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat and alarm occurring alongside shame and beliefs, but it does not explicitly convey that his sense of threat leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly state that Arjun’s sense of threat increases attention to, sensitivity to, or creation of triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: Although avoidance and other maladaptive strategies are described as narrowing his life, the vignette does not clearly state that these strategies lead to increased exposure to or sensitivity to triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette describes maladaptive strategies maintaining memories and shame, but it does not explicitly convey that these strategies heighten Arjun’s sense of threat or danger.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
